newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian March labour force data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian March labour force data.

text.p: Australian employment fell 33,900 in March and the unemployment rate was 8.7 percent, official figures showed.
Fulltime employment fell by 30,400 in the month.
Median forecasts had centred on a rise of 13,500 in employment and an unemployment rate of 8.7 percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow.
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"Well, obviously, very weak figures and they may see some concerns that policy may be moved towards an easing stance from the current neutral level. That could be the initial market reaction anyway. I think that's (the fall in full time employment) what they would really be focusing on, because we saw in February a significant fall there, down around about 24,000, two months in a row that's very significant."
TONY MEER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"Obviously, it is a surprisingly large fall (in employment) and I think it is worth noting that the number of unemployed also fell quite sharply in the month. The actual unemployment rate was down to 8.7 percent so effectively all these people just packed up and left the labour force. The first few months of 1997 appear to have been quite weak in terms of employment growth and taking that at face value it really does say the economy does have some room to grow a little faster, to use the Reserve Bank's terminology. But you have to sit that against a range of other indicators that suggest that 1997 started at quite a rapid pace -- I am talking about retail sales data, housing related statistics. So therefore you are left with the view I think that you wait for more information, wait to see if this trend is confirmed at a later date or does turn out to be strange numbers."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It certainly is a little at odds with all the other indicators of where the economy is going. All the other indicators are basically pointing to a stronger picture as we move through 1997. So it's a little difficult to rationalise today's numbers, other than to say that it is probably partly still reflecting the weakness from overall activity in late 1996. I would think we'd certainly be looking at a much stronger labour market from here on in. Certainly where job vacancies are now tells you that we should be seeing employment growth quite a deal stronger than it's been over the last couple of months."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"They are surprisingly weak, they're consistent however with the job ad series, both the ANZ series and the ABS series, and also some of the softness in the DEET survey. Even though it's picked up in the last few months, it is still at levels that aren't really conducive to a strong lift in employment. I think its a little premature (talk of a rate cut). Never forget that employment is a lagging indicator of activity and this is a response to the slowdown in 1996."
ANTHONY THOMPSON, ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"I am very, very surprised. No one could see this one coming. It certainly leaves the (employment) trend in bad shape particularly on the full time side. It is unusal to get such a weak employment result and a fall in the unemployment rate, that is only due to a sharp fall in the participation rate. If they hadn't had that fall in the participation rate the unemployment rate would have gone through nine percent with no trouble at all. It certainly means there is no pressure for a tightening."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER (AUSTRALIA):

"The thing that strikes me is that there is a pretty dreadful statistic in that the trend employment series has dropped to show that job growth is only 2,100 in a month, that is very paltry employment growth in a total number of employed persons around the 8.5 million mark. It is telling us that we have a very weak labour market out there. This is a good reason why Australia won't be following in the footsteps of Fed anytime soon."
ROBIN LARSEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"It was certainly weaker than the market expected but when you look it...it's consistent with employment rolling along at a weak growth rate. Our own job ads series would suggest no real strength in the labour market yet. Employment's the last one to turn and on our reading it's the second half of the year before you really get the flow of employment creation. There maybe speculation again about further easings but I think that's unlikely. All the partial indicators have firmed in recent months and if you ease policy again all you do is add fuel to a key sector which is recovering quite well, the housing sector."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"Clearly, there is a mixed picture emerging. We were surprised by the weakness in employment. Caton said unemployment had improved only marginally, to 8.74 percent from 8.79 percent. It's still a very weak number. But he pointed to strong retail sales growth and housing growth and said employment, a lagging indicator, would pick up. We are not going to go on with employment as weak as it is now."
CHRIS RICHARDSON, DIRECTOR, ACCESS ECONOMICS:
"In March, full-time employment was 6,246,400. The previous peak was in July 1990, at 6,236,200. So in almost seven years, full-time employment in this country has grown by merely 10,000."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
